Key Characteristics & Etiology: Cumulative blood loss >=500ml (minor 500-1000ml, major >1000ml) within 24h of delivery. Etiology: 4 Ts (Tone 80%, Tissue, Trauma, Thrombin).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Failure of uterine myometrial contraction (atony) or tissue/vascular disruption preventing mechanical vessel occlusion at placental site.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Profuse vaginal bleeding, soft boggy uterus. Red Flags: Tachycardia (>100 bpm), hypotension (SBP <90), tachypnoea, oliguria, hypovolemic shock.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Clinical estimation + blood crossmatch + FBC + Coag; Uterine massage + IV Oxytocin (Syntocinon) + IM Ergometrine (if no HTN) + IM Carboprost (if no asthma) + Misoprostol + Bakri balloon / B-Lynch

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Excessive/abnormal vaginal bleeding occurring between 24 hours and 6 weeks postpartum. Caused by retained placenta/membranes or endometritis.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Persistent retained trophoblastic tissue or intrauterine bacterial infection causing sloughing of placental bed vessels.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Persistent heavy vaginal bleeding, foul-smelling lochia, pelvic pain, low-grade fever, subinvolution of uterus.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: High vaginal & cervical swabs + Pelvic Ultrasound (RPOC detection); Broad-spectrum oral/IV antibiotics (Co-amoxiclav + Metronidazole) + surgical evacuation if RPOC confirmed.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Indenting or collapse of the uterine fundus into the uterine cavity/vagina during 3rd stage. Risk factors: fundal placenta, excessive cord traction before separation.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Inversion of uterine wall secondary to traction on umbilical cord when uterus is relaxed, leading to neurogenic and hypovolemic shock.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Severe abdominal/pelvic pain, sudden postpartum shock out of proportion to visible blood loss, vaginal mass or absent fundus on abdominal palpation.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Clinical examination; IMMEDIATE manual fundal replacement (Johnson maneuver) BEFORE placental removal or uterotonics; Tocolytics (Nitroglycerin/Terbutaline) if inverted ring tight; Oxytocin AFTER replacement.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Full-thickness disruption of myometrium and visceral peritoneum during labour. Highest risk in trial of scar (VBAC) or oxytocin misuse.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Mechanical tearing of prior Caesarean section lower segment scar under active labour contractions.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Sudden severe breakthrough abdominal pain, cessation of uterine contractions, acute CTG decelerations/bradycardia (55-87%), loss of fetal station, haematuria.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Continuous CTG + clinical exam; Stop Oxytocin immediately + emergency fluid resuscitation + Category 1 Caesarean section with uterine repair or emergency hysterectomy.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Infection of genital tract occurring from ROM/labour up to 6 weeks postpartum. Most common causative organism: Group A Streptococcus (GAS / Strep pyogenes).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Ascending bacterial infection causing acute endometritis, parametritis, pelvic peritonitis, and systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS).
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Pyrexia (>38.3C), chills/rigors, foul purulent lochia, pelvic/uterine tenderness, tachycardia (>100 bpm); Red Flag: serum lactate >4 mmol/L.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Sepsis Six Bundle within 1h: Blood cultures, Lactate, Urine output, High-flow O2, Broad-spectrum IV Antibiotics (Piperacillin/Tazobactam or Co-amoxiclav + Metronidazole), IV crystalloids.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Emergency Caesarean section indicated when there is immediate threat to maternal or fetal life. Target Decision-to-Delivery Interval (DDI) <30 minutes.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Acute irreversible fetal distress or catastrophic maternal collapse requiring immediate surgical delivery.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Profound persistent fetal bradycardia, uterine rupture, cord prolapse, severe placental abruption, uterine inversion.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Continuous CTG + Rapid multi-disciplinary response; Regional (spinal/epidural) or General Anaesthesia + Joel-Cohen/Pfannenstiel incision + single-dose IV antibiotic prophylaxis.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Urgent Caesarean section indicated when there is maternal or fetal compromise but no immediate threat to life. Target DDI <75 minutes.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Progressive non-reassuring fetal status or failure to progress in labour without immediate vascular collapse.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Pathological CTG trace without prolonged bradycardia, failure to progress / dystocia with non-reassuring CTG, failed instrumental delivery.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Continuous CTG; Spinal anaesthesia + prophylactic IV antibiotics + antacid prophylaxis (Ranitidine/Sodium citrate).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Combined ethinylestradiol + progestogen daily oral pill. UKMEC 4 absolute contraindications: Migraine with aura, BP >=160/100, VTE history, smoking >=15/day age >=35.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Inhibition of ovulation via negative feedback on LH/FSH surge + thickening of cervical mucus + endometrial thinning.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Highly effective (>99% perfect use); regulates cycles, reduces dysmenorrhea and HMB, reduces ovarian & endometrial cancer risk.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: BP & BMI assessment before initiation; UKMEC screening; standard 21/7 regimen or continuous tailored regimen.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device (Mirena/Kyleena). First-line treatment for Heavy Menstrual Bleeding (HMB); highly effective LARC for 5-8 years.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Local progestogen release causing profound endometrial atrophy, suppression of endo-myometrial vascularity, and thickening of cervical mucus.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Amenorrhea or light spotting after 3-6 months, dramatic reduction in dysmenorrhea and HMB (>90% reduction).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Bimanual exam + STI screen before insertion; insert within 7 days of menses or any time if non-pregnant; check threads post-menses.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Non-hormonal intrauterine device containing copper coils. Licensed for 5-10 years. Most effective method of emergency contraception.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Copper ions exert spermicidal action, inhibit sperm motility and fertilization, and induce inflammatory endometrial response preventing implantation.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Non-hormonal contraception; may increase menstrual blood loss and dysmenorrhea in first 3-6 months.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Pelvic exam + Chlamydia/Gonorrhea screening; can be inserted up to 5 days (120h) post-UPSI or up to 5 days post-calculated ovulation for emergency contraception.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Single oral dose 30mg selective progesterone receptor modulator (EllaOne). Effective up to 120 hours (5 days) post-unprotected intercourse.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Binds to progesterone receptors and delays or inhibits ovulation even after LH surge has begun (unlike Levonorgestrel).
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Single oral dose within 120h of UPSI; main side effect: mild nausea, delayed menses.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Contraindicated in severe asthma managed by oral steroids; avoid hormonal contraception for 5 days post-intake; repeat dose if vomiting within 3 hours.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Single oral dose 1.5mg progestogen (Levonelle). Effective up to 72 hours (3 days) post-unprotected intercourse. UKMEC 1 (no medical contraindications).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Inhibits LH surge and delays ovulation BEFORE the LH surge has started; ineffective once LH surge has commenced.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Single oral dose within 72h of UPSI; double dose (3mg) if BMI >26 or taking enzyme-inducing drugs.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: No medical contraindications (UKMEC 1); can resume regular hormonal contraception immediately.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Permanent surgical contraception via laparoscopic mechanical occlusion of bilateral fallopian tubes using Filshie clips or salpingectomy.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Mechanical blockage of fallopian tubes preventing ovum transport and sperm-egg interaction.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Permanent non-reversible decision; failure rate approx 1 in 200 (0.5%); ectopic risk if failure occurs.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Comprehensive pre-procedure counseling regarding non-reversibility and LARC alternatives; perform in follicular phase or with effective contraception.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Laceration extending into anal sphincter complex during vaginal delivery. 3rd degree (anal sphincter tear) & 4th degree (anorectal mucosa tear). Risk: instrumental birth, OP position, macrosomia.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Mechanical tearing of external anal sphincter (EAS), internal anal sphincter (IAS), and rectal mucosa during crowning.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Severe perineal pain, rectal bleeding; risk of long-term anal incontinence and flatal incontinence if misdiagnosed or inadequately repaired.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Systematic digital rectal examination post-delivery; Repair in operating theatre by trained obstetrician under regional/general anaesthesia using end-to-end or overlap PDS suture + IV antibiotics + oral laxatives.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Mediolateral episiotomy incision made at 45-60 degree angle from mid-perineum during crowning. Indicated for instrumental delivery, fetal distress, or rigid perineum.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Surgical incision through perineal skin, vaginal mucosa, and perineal muscles (bulbospongiosus & superficial transverse perineal) to enlarge vaginal introitus.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Controlled enlargement of introitus; protects against ragged 3rd/4th degree midline perineal tears.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Infiltration with 10-20ml 1% Lignocaine; 3-layer continuous suture repair (1: vaginal mucosa, 2: perineal muscle layer, 3: subcuticular perineal skin).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Natural family planning using physiological indicators (calendar/Ogino-Knaus, basal body temperature BBT, cervical mucus / Billings method).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Identification of fertile window (5 days before ovulation to 1 day after) to avoid unprotected intercourse.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Requires high user motivation and commitment; typical failure rate 15-24%.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Biphasic BBT rise of 0.2-0.5C indicates post-ovulatory phase; clear, stretchy cervical mucus (spinnbarkeit) indicates peak fertility.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Contraceptive initiation guidelines following childbirth. Women are non-fertile before Day 21 postpartum; contraception required from Day 21 (3 weeks).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Postpartum ovulation suppression via lactational amenorrhea (LAM) or physiological anovulation up to 21 days.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: LAM criteria: 100% exclusively breastfeeding, amenorrheic, and <6 months postpartum (98% effective).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Progestogen-only pill (POP) & Implant can be started immediately (Day 1); COCP strictly UKMEC 4 <21 days (VTE risk); Cu-IUD/LNG-IUS inserted within 48h or delayed to >=4 weeks.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Surgical continuous bracing suture applied around uterine body to treat refractory uterine atony during Caesarean section or laparotomy.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Provides continuous mechanical vertical compression of anterior and posterior uterine walls, tamponading open myometrial bleeding vessels.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Controls severe PPH without hysterectomy; preserves fertility.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Perform uterine re-assessment; pass 0-Monocryl / Vicryl suture vertically from lower segment over fundus and back through posterior wall; tie securely.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Intrauterine silicone balloon inserted into uterine cavity and inflated with 300-500ml warm normal saline to control atonic PPH.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Direct hydrostatic compression exerted by inflated balloon against inner uterine wall, stopping capillary and venous oozing.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: First-line conservative surgical intervention for refractory PPH failing oxytocics.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Insert balloon into uterine cavity via cervix or C-section incision; inflate with 300-500ml sterile saline; maintain oxytocin infusion; remove after 12-24 hours.

Entity / Condition: Postpartum Blues vs. Puerperal Sepsis vs. Psychosis
Key Characteristics & Etiology: Differential diagnosis of acute maternal distress in early puerperium.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Hormonal withdrawal (blues), systemic bacterial infection (sepsis), or severe psychiatric neurochemical disturbance (psychosis).
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Blues: mild lability, tearfulness d3-10, self-limiting. Sepsis: high fever, tachycardia, purulent lochia. Psychosis: delusions, paranoia, infant harm risk (d3-14).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Blues: reassurance. Sepsis: Sepsis Six + IV Antibiotics. Psychosis: Emergency psychiatric referral & admission to Mother and Baby Unit (MBU).
